title: Market Replay Studio
subtitle: Queue dynamics, inventory control and adverse selection you can inspect.

cases.label: Balanced flow
cases.title: Watch the queue. Account for every fill.
cases.description: Balanced flow: a price/time-priority book, cancellable orders, inventory-constrained quoting and stale quotes. Replay the managed policy, then compare net results across sixteen paired seeds.

charts.title: Marked equity before final liquidation · seed 1729
Liquidated outcome over independent paired seeds

method: Orders match at the resting price, best price then FIFO. Partial fills and owner-checked cancellations use the same book as the replay, with integer price/quantity accounting.

All trader accounts conserve aggregate cash and inventory after every batch. Agent fees are a separate external charge of 0.05 tick/unit; the net ledger includes that fee sink. Final liquidation executes through five refreshed LP levels, ten units each, starting at mid ±3 ticks. Price slippage and fees are included.
Inventory is bounded at ±20 units through quote sizing. Latency means quotes refresh every five batches; background liquidity and marketable external orders continue each batch.

Sixteen independent seeds compare policies with identical pre-generated price, order-size and flow draws. In the adverse regime, 70% of eligible flow is informed by the next reference move; this privileged signal is unavailable to the agent.
limitations: Synthetic event flow and exogenous reference prices are not calibrated exchange data. No claim of profitable live trading is made.
Background refreshes may trade against stale agent quotes; losses from those crossings are included. The agent does not control market impact or reference prices.
Latency is measured in event batches, not network nanoseconds. Hidden liquidity, auctions, credit limits and exchange-specific order types are omitted.
Recorded replay uses seed 1729; summary uncertainty uses separate paired seeds 100–115. Mark-to-mid equity differs from final liquidated net.

cases.label: TWAP / balanced
cases.title: Does spreading execution reduce arrival-price cost?
cases.description: Execute 120 buy units over twelve batches. Compare equal-time cumulative targets with an immediate sweep that retries residuals. Both face identical external events and finite displayed depth. Lower shortfall is better; completion and residual risk matter too.

metrics.label: TWAP arrival-price shortfall
metrics.note: Includes fees and terminal-marked unfilled opportunity cost

method: data: Synthetic; independent pre-generated external paths shared by policies
fee_per_executed_unit: 0.05
arrival: Reference midpoint before first external event
liquidity: Five levels per side, 10 units each, mid +/-3..7; fully refreshed every batch
event_order: Refresh background, external IOC, parent IOC; no resting parent remainder
shortfall: s*(notional-filled*arrival) + fees + s*residual*(terminal_mid-arrival); s=+1 buy, -1 sell
residual: Unexecuted positive parent units; marked at terminal reference, not liquidated
baseline: Release entire parent at batch zero and retry residual every batch
twap: Cumulative floor(Q*(t+1)/T) target each batch; carry deficits, no forced terminal fill
uncertainty: 16 independent paired seeds 200..215; Student t(15) 95% CI for TWAP minus baseline; negative favors TWAP
boundaries: No calibrated flow, permanent impact, latency, funding, borrow cost, hidden depth, or fee tiers
limitations: Synthetic reference prices and full background replenishment are exogenous; depth depletion is real within a batch but there is no persistent impact. Findings depend on this strong replenishment assumption.
Residual units are not trades. Their signed terminal midpoint opportunity cost is a valuation convention and does not guarantee executable completion. Negative costs are retained.
TWAP is a deterministic equal-time cumulative schedule with catch-up, not a calibrated optimal policy. The baseline can consume more depth earlier and retries until the same deadline.
Recorded replay uses seed 1729; table means and paired t intervals use independent seeds 200–215. No real-market edge is established.
